quarterly_data.signal: AGENTIC WORKLOADS ARE THE CPU DEMAND DRIVER, AND IRELAND IS THE SUPPLY ANSWER: CFO David Zinsner quantified the workload shift for the first time - comparing a regular training data center with an agentic-like activity, 'it's like a 4 to 6 increase in CPU requirements'. Server CPU units, which used to decline low single digits, are now growing double digits with core counts growing at multiples of that, and ASP per core - which fell almost 20% in some years - has at least stabilized and in some like-for-like cases is going up, so core-count growth now flows straight through to revenue. The constraint is supply, not competitive performance: 'as we look at this year, next year, probably even into 2028, this is going to be less about competitive performance of CPUs and more about can you get the CPUs to the customer', and share will follow whoever can supply. Granite Rapids, the data-center flagship, is built in Ireland on Intel 3; part of next year's CapEx is to ramp Ireland where Intel wants to 'more than double the output there next year'. Even so Intel will 'under-supply for sure this year', 'probably under-supply next year', and hopes to be in a good position by 2028.
quarterly_data.figure: 4 to 6 increase in CPU requirements; more than double the output there next year

quarterly_data.signal: MEMORY PRICING IS KILLING CLIENT DEMAND, AND INTEL DELIBERATELY REDIRECTED THAT CAPACITY TO DATA CENTER: Zinsner said Intel made a conscious decision at the beginning of the year, seeing that memory pricing would 'start to destroy some of the demand on the client side' - it focused client CPU capacity on big-core products, yielded small-core parts to others, and shifted as much supply as possible to data center on the strength of long-term agreements with data-center customers. Intel 3 cannot flex (Meteor Lake was the only client product in Ireland and is rolling off as Panther Lake ramps), so more Granite Rapids output has to come from new capacity, throughput and yields; but moving client off Intel 7 onto Intel 18A frees Intel 7 capacity that is being used to supply the data-center market. He called the client weakness 'probably the best thing we could have, given the data center demand', and expects the memory hangover to persist into next year before snapping back through 2027.

GROSS MARGIN NOW 'COMFORTABLY IN THE 40s' AND A NEW INTERNAL RULE OF 45: Zinsner said the 2026 plan submitted by the businesses was high-30s gross margin and he pushed the team into the 40s - 'I can safely say, I think, that we are now kind of comfortably in the 40s in gross margins. Low 40s' - with the goal of mid-40s, high-40s and ultimately 'something that starts with a five'. The drag he flagged: Foundry front end and advanced packaging are 'probably 40% gross margin businesses, at least for now' (still ~30s operating margin), and a lot of ASIC products are also 'kind of 40s' gross margin, so success in those high-growth businesses weighs on corporate gross margin. To manage that, Intel adopted a 'Rule of 45' (revenue growth plus operating margin) for every business unit; every unit has submitted a long-range plan that achieves it, and Lip-Bu Tan presented it as a main slide in the capital raise.
quarterly_data.figure: comfortably in the 40s; 40% gross margin businesses; Rule of 45

quarterly_data.signal: FOUNDRY BREAKEVEN TARGET END OF 2027 - BUT SUCCESS COULD PUSH IT INTO 2028: Zinsner said Intel is driving the foundry business to breakeven by the end of 2027 as its internal target, while acknowledging that winning more customers carries porting investment and startup expenses that 'could elongate the time to breakeven' - 'I could see us going into 2028 and not being there yet, and maybe it's the end of 2028 even that we get there.' Foundry operating profit has been running at 'like a $2.5 billion loss or so per quarter', and regardless of the crossover date he wants relative steady improvement every quarter. Separately he confirmed an Analyst Day is planned but not this year - sometime next year - and said investors should not expect Intel to announce foundry customers at it: 'that's not done in the foundry industry, and we're not going to be an outlier.'
quarterly_data.figure: $2.5 billion loss or so per quarter; breakeven by the end of 2027

quarterly_data.signal: THE CAPITAL RAISE IS A SUBSTRATE-AND-FAB SPENDING EVENT: Zinsner explained the August equity raise as 'the capital raise precedes capital investment' - 2026 CapEx has already been upticked 'by a couple of billion dollars from $18 billion to $20 billion', next year's will be significantly higher, and 'substrates are really constrained and we're going to need to make investments associated with substrates as well next year, given the significant demand.' Committing to 14A high-volume manufacturing in 2028 means placing long-lead supplier orders now, which was one of the biggest drivers of the raise. On footprint: Ireland's shell is being equipped now; Fab 52 in Arizona is running Intel 18A and Fab 62 is almost ready, with next year's investment accelerating its equipping; Oregon stays the pilot line but will also run volume Intel 14A as 18A is pushed into Arizona; Ohio shells are in progress with the ability to have 'eight mods, or there is two mods per fab, so four fabs in Ohio', mod one being built as fast as possible. Zinsner said 2027 CapEx is not locked - the businesses gave him a number and 'I've told them no', sending them back for more efficiency before he guides.
quarterly_data.figure: from $18 billion to $20 billion; eight mods, or there is two mods per fab, so four fabs in Ohio

quarterly_data.signal: INTEL 14A: 0.9 PDK IN OCTOBER, RISK PRODUCTION 2027, HIGH-VOLUME 2028: Zinsner said Intel is within two months of the 14A 0.9 PDK, so 'you can pretty much now expect us to land in October with that 0.9 PDK', and the remaining step from 0.9 to 1.0 is much smaller than 0.5 to 0.9. Defect density on Intel 14A is tracking better than the target curve and is coming down faster than any previous node - 'we haven't seen this performance since 22 nanometer, which is arguably one of the best nodes Intel's ever put out' - while 18A yields are beating internal milestones. Demand side: internal product teams, 'probably the most cynical bunch out of anybody', are now designing products on Intel 14A, and external foundry engagements have increased enough that Lip-Bu Tan and the team meet customers weekly and the conversation has moved from data to 'how much capacity can I get? What does that supply look like?'. That sequence forces risk production in 2027 ahead of high-volume manufacturing in 2028.
quarterly_data.figure: 0.9 PDK in October; risk production in 2027; high volume production in 2028; 22 nanometer

quarterly_data.signal: EMIB-T ADVANCED PACKAGING SIZED FOR THE FIRST TIME - REVENUE FROM 2H 2027, MULTIPLE BILLIONS PER CUSTOMER: Zinsner said EMIB-T, which removes the interposer from EMIB and can increase reticle size significantly, is a differentiated solution not available elsewhere, and that packaging revenue will 'start to ramp in the back half of 2027', become a run-rate business in 2028 and be 'definitely hitting its stride in 2029'. Scale: 'this business is in the billions... by customer, it will be multiple billion dollars per customer per year of business', at margins of '40% gross, 30% operating margin' with low capital intensity relative to the front end, so 'the ROIC is phenomenal'. He framed advanced packaging as the on-ramp that tests Intel operationally and creates cross-sell into front-end foundry, something Intel has 'already seen that show up even now'. He also pointed to the hire of Seokhee, former CEO of SK hynix, to lead the business as the signal of the opportunity size.
quarterly_data.figure: back half of 2027; multiple billion dollars per customer per year; 40% gross, 30% operating margin
